newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand markets nervous over power of Peters.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand markets nervous over power of Peters.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar opened lower on Wednesday on concern over the powerful role of populist leader Winston Peters as Treasurer in a centre-right coalition government.
But rating agency Moody's, other markets and newspaper editorials approved the deal.

Holding the balance of power, Peters on Tuesday chose the conservative National Party as his coalition partner over the left-leaning Labour Party in a dramatic selection process after eight weeks of painful deliberations.

There was bitter reaction from many people and organisations, including trade unions and pensioners, who believed Peters had betrayed them after vehemently fighting the National party in the October 12 election.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger's car was extensively damaged after being torched in an incident overnight. Police were investigating, and the diplomatic protection squad said it was stepping up security for Bolger and other leaders.
Foreign exchange dealers said they were wary of the populist and flamboyant Peters because of his anti-foreign investment views and proclivity for interventionism.

"The (forex) market initially responded to the blue (conservative) flag being waved, but then a sense of reality struck home that Winston Peters was the Treasurer," said National Bank chief foreign exchange dealer Stu Nattrass.

"The markets are struggling with the credibility of Peters as Treasurer given his views on foreign investment and the relative value of the exchange rate and the level of expenditure he desires. It's very difficult to see interest rates charging on (lower)," he said.
The "kiwi" dollar, after initially surging on news that National was chosen, dropped about one U.S. cent to 69.7 cents by late morning.
Other markets were more enthusiastic. The share market market opened 1.1 percent up and short-term interest rates fell half a percentage point to just above 7.9 percent.
Moody's Senior Analyst Yves Lemay told Reuters New Zealand's rating profile remained "firmly in the AA-1 rating category for its foreign currency debt and AAA for its domestic debt".
"The bottom line from our perspective is we don't anticipate new players in a new government would have any material impact on the rating," he said.

He played down market concerns about smaller budget surpluses and changing of the central Reserve Bank's targets to include sustainable growth and to widen the inflation goal to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent.
Newspaper editorials saw the agreement on the coalition as signalling the start of a new era for New Zealand under its new proporotional electoral system, and they were approving.

"While Mr Peters so far is the personal winner in the drawn-out formation of this coalition government, the best possible result has also been achieved for New Zealand as a whole," wrote the Otago Daily Times.
But the country's biggest paper, The New Zealand Herald, noted that National had paid a heavy price in giving away the Treasury job.
"That looks like the very sell-out some people had feared," it said.
